'''Joseph Lee Rodgers III''' (born February 9, 1953)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/n86843232.html |title=Rodgers, Joseph Lee, 1953- |website=Library of Congress Name Authority File |access-date=2018-07-31}}</ref> is an American psychologist who specializes in quantitative psychology and topics in developmental psychology and social biology. He is the Lois Autrey Betts Professor of Psychology and Human Development Emeritus at [[Vanderbilt University]], and he is also the [[George Lynn Cross]] Research Professor Emeritus at the [[University of Oklahoma]], where he taught from 1981 to 2012. 

==Education and career==
Rodgers graduated from the [[University of Oklahoma]] in 1975 with a B.S. in mathematics and a B.A. in psychology. He received his Ph.D. in [[quantitative psychology]] from the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] in 1981, with a minor in [[biostatistics]]. His dissertation was on the effects of family configuration on mental development.

He is a past president of the [[Society for the Study of Social Biology]], the [[Society of Multivariate Experimental Psychology]], and Divisions 5 and 34 of the [[American Psychological Association]]. From 2006 to 2011, he was [[editor-in-chief]] of ''[[Multivariate Behavioral Research]]''. He has been a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] since 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.vanderbilt.edu/psychological_sciences/bio/joe-rodgers |title=Joseph Lee Rodgers |website=Vanderbilt University |language=en |access-date=2018-07-31}}</ref> 

His substantive research has focused on topics such as the relationship between [[birth order]] and [[human intelligence]],<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/02/14/books/what-runs-in-the-family-isn-t-success.html |title=What Runs In the Family Isn't Success |last=Eakin |first=Emily |date=2004-02-14 |work=The New York Times |access-date=2018-07-31 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.slate.com/articles/life/family/2007/06/out_of_order.html |title=Out of Order |last=Bazelon |first=Emily |date=2007-06-26 |work=Slate |access-date=2018-07-31 |language=en-US |issn=1091-2339}}</ref> as well as adolescent risk behaviors, like sexual activity and drug use.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://newsok.com/article/2364993/summer-sexy-time-for-teens |title=Summer Sexy Time for Teens |date=1991-08-07 |work=NewsOK.com |access-date=2018-07-31 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |url=http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,1209949-5,00.html |title=The New Science of Siblings |last=Kluger |first=Jeffrey |date=2006-07-10 |magazine=Time |access-date=2018-07-31 |language=en-US |issn=0040-781X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-10-21-ls-56100-story.html |title=The Path of No Return |last=Roan |first=Shari |date=1996-10-21 |work=Los Angeles Times |access-date=2018-07-31 |language=en-US |issn=0458-3035|page=2}}</ref> His methodological research focuses on behavior genetics, exploratory data analysis,<ref>Fife, D. A., & Rodgers, J. L. (2022). Understanding the exploratory/confirmatory data analysis continuum: Moving beyond the "replication crisis". ''American Psychologist, 77''(3), 453–466. {{doi|10.1037/amp0000886}}</ref> correlation and regression,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rodgers |first1=Joseph Lee |last2=Nicewander |first2=W. Alan |date=1988-02-01 |title=Thirteen Ways to Look at the Correlation Coefficient |url=https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.1988.10475524 |journal=The American Statistician |volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=59–66 |doi=10.1080/00031305.1988.10475524 |issn=0003-1305|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hadd |first1=Alexandria Ree |url=https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/understanding-correlation-matrices/book263182 |title=Understanding correlation matrices |date=2021 |last2=Rodgers |first2=Joseph Lee|isbn=978-1-5443-4110-1 |location=Los Angeles |oclc=1289850692}}</ref> and best practices for research methods.<ref>Rodgers, J. L. & Shrout, P. E.(2018). Psychology’s replication crisis as scientific opportunity: A précis for policymakers. ''Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 5(1)'', 134-141. {{doi|10.1177/2372732217749254}}.</ref>
